rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 (Materials and Methods; Results) - the authors build a mobile variable-rate drip line prototype and run their own laboratory tests measuring applied depths with collectors, uniformity (CUC 95-98%), displacement speed and hose pressure loss.
rows.notes: The study contains no AI, predictive analytics, real-time weather or soil-moisture data, or scheduling app. Required depths are pre-computed from reference ET and Kc and loaded by the user onto an SD card; the prototype then applies them at variable rate via valve pulses and line speed. The 'potential water savings' of 23.2% (at least 19.1%) in Section 3.3 is a calculation comparing average required depth with the maximum depth a constant-rate system would apply, not a measured reduction from AI-driven scheduling. The 'up to 30%' figure does not appear in the study.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 - own laboratory evaluation of a prototype mobile drip line (CUC under constant and variable rates, application efficiency 93.4% at GA 83%, speed variation, pressure loss).
rows.notes: The study does test a drip line, but its water-use result is about the variable-rate control feature, not drip irrigation as such: the 23.2% (>=19.1%) 'potential water savings' in Section 3.3 is computed as the difference between average required depth and the maximum depth that a constant-rate version of the same drip line would apply. Drip is not compared with any other irrigation method, the savings are a desk calculation on lab-collected depths rather than a measured field reduction, and there is no IoT (only local 2.4 GHz radio between two Arduino panels), AI or remote sensing. Q9 note: SD/CV are reported for CUC and relative depth (95 <U+00B1> 1.4%; 1.05 <U+00B1> 0.05), but not for the water-savings figure; irrelevant since Q2 is no.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 - own laboratory tests of a prototype variable-rate mobile drip line.
rows.notes: No remote sensing (satellite, UAV or proximal sensors) is used anywhere in the study; crop water needs are entered manually from ET0 and Kc values on an SD card. The only mention of remote sensing is a cited UAV-based VRI study [26] in the Discussion, which does not count. The study's water-savings figure is a calculated potential for variable-rate versus constant-rate application.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 - own laboratory tests of a prototype variable-rate mobile drip line (uniformity, application efficiency, speed and pressure loss).
rows.notes: No scheduling app, IoT platform, AI or sensor-based scheduling is tested; the Arduino control reads user-prepared depth tables from an SD card and controls line speed and valve pulses. The tested technology is variable-rate application hardware, not app-based scheduling, and the 23.2% potential savings is a calculation against a hypothetical constant-rate application rather than a measured scheduling outcome.

notes: Full text available (some pages are garbled by PDF layout duplication but all sections are readable). The study is a laboratory prototype development and hydraulic/uniformity evaluation of a mobile variable-rate drip line for diversified vegetable beds; it does not involve AI, apps, IoT connectivity, remote sensing, or real-time weather/soil-moisture inputs, and reports no measured field water savings (only a calculated potential saving relative to constant-rate application). The authors themselves state that further study is needed to quantify resource savings (Conclusions).
